newsitem.title: USA: Cocoa climbs to nine-year high, copper tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa climbs to nine-year high, copper tumbles.

text.p: Cocoa prices stormed to a nine-year high on Tuesday on speculative buying sparked partly by growing concern about the possible impact on crops of a developing "El Nino" weather pattern.
"The specs (speculators) are getting hotter and hotter for it," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "And as long as there's talk of El Nino, cocoa will have a nice run."

El Nino is a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean off South America that has widespread consequences for global weather. Analysts fear that crops from Indonesia to West Africa could be hit by dry conditions due to the developing weather pattern.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, cocoa for July delivery rose to a peak of $1,700 a metric ton, the highest level for a nearby contract since May 1988. July closed $17 up on the day at $1,680.
Some traders cautioned that it was too early to gauge the effects of El Nino on next year's harvest.
Crop-boosting heavy rains were also reported in Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer and exporter.
"Soil moisture is now back to normal from the north to the south," said a national weather station spokesman in Abidjan. "The weather has been good."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, copper prices sank to a six-week low as the U.S. physical market succumbed to a seasonal summer slowdown.
Copper for July delivery fell to a low of 111.60 cents a lb before closing 6.05 cents weaker at 112.15 cents.
"There were no buyers out there and just selling into vacuum," John Tyree of FIMAT Futures said. "We started to break new technical levels and everyone headed for the exit at the same time."

Crude oil also closed lower on the New York Mercantile Exchange as early-session strength evaporated after Iraq's oil minister said he expected his country to resume oil exports in the next week to 10 days.
August crude settled 11 cents off at $19.03 a barrel. July gasoline ended 0.04 cent up at 55.68 cents a gallon, while July heating oil finished off 0.35 cent at 51.57 cents a gallon.

At a news conference in Madrid on Tuesday, Iraqi oil minister Amir Rasheed said Iraq expected to resume oil exports under a pact with the United Nations that allows Iraq to sell oil in exchange for humanitarian aid.

The U.N. allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil in the six months ended May 30 under a deal that partially relaxes Gulf War sanctions. The program was extended for a further six months but oil sales have been delayed.

"The market couldn't penetrate the upper end of its range, and Rasheed's statements were simply justification for taking this market lower," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Although Iraqi exports will add a large amount of supply, some dealers wondered whether exports could resume so soon in view of logistical problems.
"It is significant that crude settled above $19.00 since it shows the market is skeptical of Rasheed's comments," Brown said.

Volume was moderate, however, as dealers avoided taking large positions ahead of a summer meeting of ministers of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries in Vienna that officially starts Wednesday.

Traders expect OPEC ministers to extend the group's self-imposed production ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day even though widespread quota-busting has boosted OPEC output two million barrels above that level.
